Walker, Horatio, painter. 

B. Listowel, Ont., 1858; studied 
miniature painting in the studio of 
the late J. A. Fraser, Toronto; later, 
went to N. Y., where “by dint of in- 
born talent and careful and con- 
ecientious study of the best available 
examples of art, he has earned for 
himself a creditable position in the 
ranks of Am. artists” (Vide W. Lewis 
Fraser, Century, Nov., 1893); ‘an 
engraving of one of his paintings, 
“A Morning in Spring,” is given in 
the same number of the Century; an 
exhibition of 30 of his pictures was 
given at the new Cottier Galleries, 
84th St., N. Y., 1897; is described in 
the N. Y. Collector as a painter of 
the pasture and the farm, and that 
he paints them very much in the feel- 
ing of a Troyon, on one hand, and 
a Mauve on the other; one of his pic- 
tures, “A Siesta,” is a marvel of the 
triumph of art over its subject; 
among his works are: ‘(Swine Herd 
and Pigs,” “ The Prodigal Son,” ‘ The 
Barnyard.” ‘ October Morning,” “ Har- 
rowing,” “Hauling the Log—Winter,” 
“Calves in Spring,” “Moonrise,” “The 
Watering Place,’ and ‘ Plowing—the 
First Gleam,” which latter won gold 
meds. at Buffalo and St. Louis 
Expns.; each of these has been 
spoken of as a work of delightful 
sentiment and feeling; was awarded 
the gold med. of the Penn. Acad. of 
Fine Arts for the general quality of 
his work, 1906; some of his pictures 
have been added to tthe Nat. Gallery, 
Ottawa; has a studio at Ste. Petro- 
nille, P.Q., where he spends from 6 to 
8\ mths. each year; a mem. Can. Art 
Club, Soc. of Am. Artists, Water Colour 
Soc., Nat. Acad. of Design, of _ the 
Royal Inst. of Painters in Water 
Colours, London, Eng.—Ste. Petronille- 
de-Beaulieu, Ile @Orleans, P.Q.

continent.”—Z7'. Globe.

tention, as well in Gt. Brit. and the 
U.S. as in Can., and did much to give 
a quietus to the Commercial Unisn fad; 
among those who complimented the 
author on their production was Sir 
John Macdonald, then Prime Minister 
of Can.; in 1902 appeared his magnum 
opus, “ Public Men and Public Life in 
Canada,’ which tells the story of the 
Confederation of Can., written in what 
the Toronto Globe declared to be “a 
fair and kindly spirit’; at an earlier 
period, produced a pamphlet on “ The 
British Preference and Imp. Federa- 
tion”; is well and favourably known 
as a public speaker, and has delivered 
many addresses and lectures in various 
portions of Ont.; among these was an 
address on “Can. Nationality: a 
Glance at the Present and the Future,” 
delivered before the National Club, 
Toronto, during the winter, 1890-91; it 
was, with other addresses, published by 
the club in book-form, and is de- 
scribed as “a vigorous and eloquent 
argument, setting forth the progress. 
and success of the Can. Confederation, 
strongly opposing any form of an- 
nexation, and advocating Can. nation- 
ality as the ultimate destiny of the 
Dom. and the best antidote to Ameri- 
ecanizing tendencies’: is an hon. mem. 
of the Can. Press Assn. ; a Lib., and one 
of Mackenzie’s “‘Old Guard”; later, 
a follower of Edward Blake and Sir 
Oliver Mowat, and now a personal 
friend and admirer of Sir Wilfrid 
Laurier; aS a young man, sat as a 
mem. of the Galt Public Sch. Bd. and 
the Co. Council; was returned for S. 
Waterloo (H.C.), at Confederation, 
and continued to represent the same 
riding up to 1878, when defeated; 
while there, was chairman of two of 
the most important standing comtes. 
of the House: Public Accounts and the

luncheon, where he delivers a message 
from His Majesty the King; says that 
“he has only one great wish and that 
is to serve Canada, to make himself 
at home in this country and to do all 
that he can to promote its best in- 
terests and also to promote that con- 
nection with the Empire which is best 








and most desirable for all’’; reaches 
Ottawa, Oct. 14; opens Parliament, 
Nov. 16; holds first Drawing Room, 
Nov. 18; pays an official visit to To- 
ronto, Nov. 27; receives hon. degree of 
LL.D. from Toronto Univ, Nov. 29% 
opens grand ball given by the Royal 
Canadian Yacht Club, same day; visits 
Hamilton, Nov. 30; visits Royal Mili- 
tary College, Kingston, Dec. 2; pays 
an official visit to Montreal, Dec. 12; 
receives hon. degree of LL.D., both for 
himself and for the Duchess of Con- 
naught, from McGill University, Dec. 
14; opens grand ball of the St. An- 
drew’s Society, Dec. 14; his daughter, 
Princess Patricia, arrives at Halifax, 
Dec. 8, and reaches Ottawa, Dec. 9; 
holds New Year Levee, Jan. 1, 1912; 
with the Duchess and the Princess 
Patricia, visits N. Y., as the guest of 
Hon. Whitelaw Reid, American .Am- 
bassador to the Court of St. James, and 
later pays an unofficial visit to Presi- 
dent Taft, at Washington, Jan. 22, 
1912; ina ‘speech at a “banquet tendered 
him ‘at Washington he said he fully 
agreed with the cordial references of 
the Secretary of State to the nature 
of the relations which now exist and 
ever will exist between the United 
States and the British Empire. As 
Governor-General of Canada he felt 
that he might give assurances that 
whatever political or party chamges 
might take place in Canada, there had 
not been and’ would not be any inten- 
tion of indicating any feeling other 
than that of closest friendship with the 
American people. The Duke concluded 
by saying that he had much enjoyed 
the opportunity given him by his visit 
of making the acquaintance of the head 
of the American State, of its President, 
Mr. Taft. The welcome which the 
President had given him had still fur- 
ther increased his satisfaction at ob- 
taining the opportunity of meeting him. 
It was therefore his very great plea- 
sure to have the honour of proposing 
the health of the President of the 
United States.
